method: Headlines from the source feed, read by Claude: summary and four beats in Blue Street's own words from each article's headline and public text; impact = which way the headline pushes each market (dir bullish/bearish/mixed, strength 1 mild, 2 clear, 3 strong). Evidence, not a call.

USD.text: Friday's jobs report, with 165,000 new jobs in October, gave the dollar its best day since June, and two senior Federal Reserve officials said more rate rises are likely needed. Markets see about an 80% chance of a rise in December, so Tuesday's October inflation figures, expected to show prices up 0.3% on the month, are the week's main test.

EUR.text: The euro slipped back to about $1.115 on Friday as a strong US jobs report lifted the dollar. At home, shop sales fell far more than expected in September, and the European Central Bank's chief economist Philip Lane sounded cautious, so a December rate rise looks less certain even with inflation near 4%.

GBP.text: The Bank of England raised its rate to 4% on Thursday, its first rise since 2023, and warned another could follow while the Iran war keeps energy costs high, which supports the pound. But on Friday a strong US jobs report lifted the dollar and pushed the pound down about 0.7% to near $1.336.

JPY.text: The yen reached its strongest in a week, near 157.4 per dollar, on Friday as Tokyo stocks fell about 6% and investors sought safety, and Bank of Japan minutes kept a December rate rise in view. A much stronger US jobs report and a bounce in US stocks pull the other way, and dearer oil, which Japan imports almost entirely, still weighs on the currency.

CHF.text: The franc drew safe-haven money last week as stocks sold off, and weekend attacks on tankers near Hormuz plus tougher talk from Iran's Revolutionary Guards keep war risk alive as markets reopen. Softer words from both Washington and Tehran on Sunday about a deal take a little of that away, and Swiss inflation at 1.5% makes a December rate cut by the Swiss National Bank harder to justify.

CAD.text: Canada lost jobs for a second month in October and unemployment rose to 6.7%, which weakens the case for another Bank of Canada rate rise; a business survey showing steady growth and more hiring only partly offsets that. With the US dollar stronger after its own jobs report and oil down sharply on the week, the Canadian dollar is under pressure.

AUD.text: The Australian dollar ended last week below 69 US cents, down about 2.4% and the weakest of the major currencies, as a crash in US chip stocks and a strong US jobs report hit it. The Reserve Bank of Australia's rate rise to 4.85% did not help much, and the bank's softer view of growth suggests few more rises are coming.

NZD.text: The New Zealand dollar fell about 1.2% on Friday, the most of the major currencies, as a strong US jobs report lifted the US dollar, and the country's jobless rate is already at its highest since 2015. Saturday's election left Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's three-party bloc with a one-seat majority that special votes could still erase, so who governs may not be clear until November 27.

XAU.text: Gold fell about 1% to near $4,050 an ounce on Friday after a strong US jobs report made a December Federal Reserve rate rise more likely; higher rates weigh on gold because it pays no interest. War risk around Iran still gives it some support, and Tuesday's US inflation figures will matter most.

OIL.text: Brent crude ended last week about 13% lower, near $98 a barrel, on hopes the Iran war is winding down. On Sunday President Trump said new US strikes are unlikely while talks progress and Iran's foreign minister said its offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days still stands, but ships keep getting hit near the strait, Iran's military is talking tougher, and a record amount of oil is stuck at sea.

items.headline: Trump says new US attacks on Iran are very unlikely as long as peace talks keep moving forward
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: US President Donald Trump told CNN on Sunday he is very unlikely to order fresh attacks on Iran while talks to end the war make progress. He tied that to Iran signing what he called a very strong agreement.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war for months, with the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that carries much of the world's oil, largely shut. Talks in Qatar have produced a draft deal, but on Friday the US hit an Iranian air-defence site and over the weekend Iran said several tankers caught fire near Hormuz.
beats.happened: In a Sunday phone interview with CNN, Trump said renewed US strikes were very unlikely if negotiations keep progressing, provided Iran agrees to a strong deal. He also said the US has picked out possible targets, including 38 bridges it could destroy within an hour. No agreement has been announced.
beats.means: It is a softer tone than last week's talk of fresh strikes, but it comes with conditions and a clear threat. It lowers the near-term risk of a new round of fighting without settling the war or reopening Hormuz.
beats.fx: Less chance of new strikes takes a little of the war premium out of oil and safe havens like gold and the Swiss franc. Ship attacks near Hormuz pull the other way, so Monday's reopening will show which weighs more.

impact.why: Fewer odds of new US strikes ease some fear of fresh supply losses, though nothing is signed.
Calmer war talk trims demand for the franc as a safe place to park money.
Gold loses a little of its war-risk support if strikes look less likely.
Cheaper oil helps Japan, which imports almost all of its energy, but calmer markets cut safe-haven demand for the yen.

items.watch: Whether Iran answers the draft deal from the Qatar talks, and any new attacks on ships near Hormuz.

items.headline: Iran's foreign minister says its offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days still stands
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that Tehran's offer to the US, which would reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days, is still on the table. He said the decision now sits with the White House, and warned Iran would hit back if the US chose war.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war for months, and the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil, is close to shut. Through mediators in Qatar, Iran has offered a two-day plan: the US eases its naval blockade and frees some Iranian money, and Iran lets ships through Hormuz again.
beats.happened: Araghchi wrote on X on Sunday evening that the offer remains in force. He said US voters had already spoken in last week's midterm elections, so it is now up to the White House, and he set an end to fighting on all fronts as part of the terms. He also warned of a military answer if Washington picks war. The US has not publicly replied.
beats.means: Both sides are now saying the door is open: President Trump said earlier on Sunday new strikes are unlikely while talks progress. That keeps a deal possible, but nothing is agreed and Iran's terms go wider than Hormuz.
beats.fx: Any real sign the strait could reopen would pull oil lower and help energy importers such as Japan and the euro area. Until the US answers, the risk of more fighting keeps some support under oil, gold and the Swiss franc.

impact.why: Iran repeats it could reopen Hormuz in two days, but the offer is not new and the US has not replied.
Japan buys almost all its energy abroad, so a path to cheaper oil helps the yen a little.
Canada exports oil, so talk of more supply getting through weighs slightly on its currency.

items.watch: A public US reply to the two-day offer, or fresh attacks on ships near Hormuz.

items.headline: A record 1.28 billion barrels of oil sit on tankers at sea as the Hormuz shutdown snarls shipping
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Crude held on tankers has hit a record of about 1.28 billion barrels, up roughly 16%, as the Iran war forces longer routes and slower transfers. Shipping now makes up a far bigger share of what a barrel costs.

beats.was: With the Strait of Hormuz largely shut by the Iran war, oil from the Gulf has to take longer, costlier paths, and countries have drawn down their stored oil. Brent crude fell sharply last week to near $98 a barrel on hopes the war is ending.
beats.happened: A market newsletter, The Kobeissi Letter, counts a record 1.28 billion barrels of crude on ships, up from about 1.1 billion. The head of Abu Dhabi's state oil company, Sultan Al Jaber, said earlier this month that shipping has risen from under 5% to over 30% of a barrel's cost, and that close to a billion barrels have come out of global stocks.
beats.means: A lot of oil is in transit rather than reaching refineries quickly, while stockpiles are thinner. That keeps supply fragile even if prices dipped last week.
beats.fx: This adds to the case that oil stays costly, which tends to help oil exporters like Canada and hurt big importers like Japan. It is a background figure rather than fresh news, so the push is mild.

impact.why: Thinner stockpiles and slow shipping keep supply tight beneath last week's price drop.
Canada sells a lot of oil abroad, so costly oil supports its currency.
Japan buys nearly all its oil abroad, so higher costs weigh on the yen.

items.watch: Whether tankers start moving through Hormuz again, and how fast global oil stocks are being drawn down.

items.headline: US October inflation figures on Tuesday are the week's big test for a December Fed rate rise
items.story_title: Fed: will it raise rates in December?
items.summary: US consumer prices for October come out Tuesday, with forecasters expecting a 0.3% monthly rise after 0.6% in September. Markets see about an 80% chance the Federal Reserve raises rates at its December 8–9 meeting.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve, the US central bank, has been weighing another rate rise because inflation is still too high. Last Friday's jobs report, with 165,000 new jobs in October, made a December rise look much more likely and gave the dollar its best day since June.
beats.happened: A weekly preview lists the US consumer price index for October on Tuesday, November 10, expected to rise 0.3% on the month, or 0.2% leaving out food and energy. Producer prices follow Friday, and more than a dozen Fed officials speak during the week. US stocks fell about 3% last week on worries about spending on AI data centres.
beats.means: With a December rate rise mostly expected, Tuesday's figures mainly decide whether that view holds. A hot reading would lock it in; a soft one would revive doubts.
beats.fx: This is a preview, not news yet. Inflation at or above forecast would back the dollar and weigh on gold, which pays no interest; a clear miss would do the reverse.

impact.why: The dollar's next move hangs on whether inflation confirms a December rate rise.
Gold usually falls when US rate-rise odds go up and gains when they fade.

items.watch: Tuesday's US consumer price figures against the 0.3% forecast, and what Fed officials say about December afterwards.

items.headline: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say three more tankers caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: The naval arm of Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three tankers exploded and burned in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday morning after using a route Iran had not approved. It warned other ships working with US forces would meet the same end.

beats.was: The US and Israel have been at war with Iran since late February. Iran lets ships through the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil, only on routes it approves, while the US blockades Iran's ports and escorts tankers through. Oil fell about 13% last week on hopes of a deal, and on Saturday two tankers were reported hit by mines.
beats.happened: On Sunday the Guards' navy said three tankers had exploded and caught fire since early morning on an unapproved channel, with smoke covering the strait. It said the ships had switched off their tracking systems and were helped by the US military, and it did not name them. Separately, a British shipping-safety agency reported tanker incidents off Oman on Saturday, and UAE state media said 22 people were rescued from a burning ship in the Gulf of Oman.
beats.means: Ship attacks near Hormuz are picking up, not easing, just as Iran weighs Qatar's plan to reopen the strait. Iran is signalling that US-escorted traffic will stay a target until a deal is done.
beats.fx: When markets reopen Sunday evening, more burning tankers add to the case for oil to win back some of last week's drop. That tends to help the Canadian dollar, gold and the franc, and weigh on the yen, since Japan imports nearly all its oil.

impact.why: Five tankers reported hit in two days puts supply risk back in the oil price after a 13% weekly fall.
A higher oil bill weighs on Japan, which buys almost all its oil abroad.
Dearer oil lifts Canada's export earnings.
More attacks at sea tend to draw safe-haven money to the franc.
Gold usually gains when the war looks set to drag on.

items.watch: How far oil rebounds when trading reopens Sunday evening, and whether Iran answers Qatar's plan before more ships are hit.

items.headline: Saudi Aramco's office tower in Riyadh is damaged as Saudi Arabia shoots down Houthi missiles from Yemen
items.story_title: Gulf: attacks spread beyond Hormuz
items.summary: Debris from intercepted missiles blew out windows in Saudi Aramco's tower in Riyadh on Sunday. Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said damage was minor and no one was hurt; oil output was not reported affected.

beats.was: Yemen's Houthi rebels, who are allied with Iran, have been firing at Saudi Arabia during the Iran war, and an Aramco site south of Riyadh was set on fire in early October. Saudi Arabia is the world's largest oil exporter, and Aramco is its state oil company.
beats.happened: On Sunday the Saudi-led coalition said it shot down several ballistic and cruise missiles aimed at Riyadh, the south of the country and the Eastern Province, where most Saudi oil is produced. Falling debris hit Aramco's office tower in Riyadh's financial district. The Houthis said they had targeted Aramco sites, Riyadh airport and military bases; that claim has not been checked.
beats.means: The war is reaching the Gulf's biggest oil producer, not just ships near Hormuz. This time the damage was to an office, not to wells or export terminals.
beats.fx: It adds a little to the supply worries already lifting oil before markets reopen Sunday evening. That leans toward the Canadian dollar and gold, and against the yen, as Japan imports nearly all its oil.

impact.why: Missiles aimed at Saudi oil areas raise supply worries, though no output was lost.
The war spreading to Saudi Arabia keeps safe-haven demand for gold alive.
Any lift to oil prices raises Japan's import bill.

items.watch: Whether the Houthis hit Saudi oil sites or export terminals, rather than offices; damage to production would be a much bigger deal for oil.

items.headline: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say they have dropped their own 2,000 km limit on missile range
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: A spokesman for Iran's Revolutionary Guards said the country no longer holds itself to a 2,000 km cap on how far its ballistic missiles can fly. Iran is not known to have longer-range missiles yet, so for now this is a threat more than a new capability.

beats.was: For years Iran said it kept its ballistic missiles to a range of about 2,000 km, roughly enough to reach Israel and US bases in the Gulf but not Europe. The country has been at war with the US for months, and Iran's supreme leader recently warned any threat would be met with a response without geographic limits.
beats.happened: At a news conference in Tehran, Revolutionary Guards spokesman General Hossein Mohebbi said the cap has been lifted. He gave no sign that a longer-range missile exists, and outside experts say none is known. US officials have warned before that Iran's space-rocket work could be turned toward longer-range missiles.
beats.means: It is a harder tone at the same time as Iran says its peace offer stands, so it reads as pressure on Washington rather than a change on the ground. It adds to the worry that the war could widen if talks fail.
beats.fx: Tougher talk from Tehran keeps some war-risk support under oil, gold and the Swiss franc. With no new weapon shown, the effect is small next to whether the talks deliver a deal.

impact.why: A harder line from Iran's military adds to the risk the war drags on, though nothing changed on the ground.
More war worry tends to send some money to the franc for safety.
Gold gains a little support from higher war risk.

items.watch: Any Iranian test of a longer-range missile, or whether the threat fades if the Qatar talks produce a deal.

items.headline: The Australian dollar ends the week below 69 US cents, the weakest major currency, despite a rate rise
items.story_title: Australian dollar: rate rise vs global sell-off
items.summary: The Australian dollar lost about 2.4% last week to near 68.7 US cents, its first weekly close below 69 cents since July. Only the Swiss franc gained against the US dollar.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of Australia, the country's central bank, raised its main rate on Tuesday to 4.85%, its fifth rise this year and the highest since 2008. A higher rate usually helps a currency.
beats.happened: A weekly currency wrap shows the Australian dollar fell the most of the major currencies anyway. A crash in US chip stocks hit risk appetite, and a strong US jobs report on Friday lifted the US dollar. The bank also said growth has slowed and house prices are down nearly 5% from their March peak.
beats.means: The rate rise was outweighed by a global flight from risk. The bank's softer view of growth also hints the run of rises may be near its end.
beats.fx: Headline pressure on the Australian dollar stays down while stocks are shaky and US rates look set to rise. The Swiss franc, the week's only gainer against the US dollar, shows where nervous money went.

impact.why: A global stock sell-off and a stronger US dollar outweighed the Reserve Bank's rate rise.
The franc was the only major currency to gain on the US dollar last week as investors sought safety.

items.watch: Whether US stocks steady this week, and Tuesday's US inflation figures, which could push the US dollar further either way.

items.headline: Blasts reported near the Strait of Hormuz and two tankers hit mines, as the US widens its blockade of Iran to land routes
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Iranian state media reported explosions on Qeshm Island and at the port of Jask on Saturday, and Iran's military said two tankers caught fire after hitting mines. The US set up a new task force to stop Iranian trade over land, while Iran studies Qatar's peace proposals.

beats.was: The US and Israel have been at war with Iran since late February, and Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, largely shut, while the US blockades Iran's ports. Oil fell about 13% last week on hopes of a deal, and on Friday President Trump said US forces made a small new strike on an Iranian air defense site.
beats.happened: On Saturday evening Iranian state media reported two blasts on Qeshm Island and several at Jask, with the cause unclear. Iran's military said two tankers caught fire after hitting mines on a route it had not approved, and the US military said it disabled a ship in the Gulf of Oman that ignored warnings. US Central Command launched Task Force Iron Gate to block weapons and sanctioned goods moving across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea, and Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it no longer limits the range of its missiles. Iran is still reviewing proposals carried by Qatar, but officials say it won't discuss its nuclear program until the US meets several conditions.
beats.means: The weekend brought more pressure from both sides, not less: mines and ship incidents near Hormuz, a wider US blockade, and tougher talk from Tehran, while the Qatari plan is still only under review.
beats.fx: Markets reopen Sunday evening. Tankers hitting mines and a tighter blockade could push oil back up after last week's big drop, which tends to help the Canadian dollar and safe havens like the franc and gold, and hurt oil importers like Japan.

impact.why: Tankers hitting mines near Hormuz and a wider US blockade add back supply risk after a 13% weekly fall.
Rising war risk tends to draw safe-haven money to the franc.
Gold usually gains when the war looks set to drag on.
Dearer oil lifts Canada's export earnings.
Japan buys almost all its oil abroad, so a higher oil bill weighs on the yen.

items.watch: Whether Iran accepts the Qatari first steps, which would reopen Hormuz in exchange for the US easing its blockade, or whether more ships are hit before markets reopen.

items.headline: New Zealand's election ends nearly tied: Labour edges the party vote, but Prime Minister Luxon's bloc holds a one-seat majority
items.story_title: New Zealand election: who governs next
items.summary: Labour won 29.4% of the party vote against National's 29.2% in Saturday's preliminary count, but National, ACT and NZ First together hold 67 of 131 seats, one more than needed. About 400,000 special votes are still to come, with the official result on November 27.

beats.was: Christopher Luxon's National Party has led a three-party government with ACT and NZ First since 2023. Polls before Saturday's vote showed a close race with Chris Hipkins' Labour, and unemployment is at its highest since 2015.
beats.happened: The Electoral Commission's election-night count, covering almost all ordinary votes, put Labour narrowly ahead on the party vote, 29.36% to 29.21%. On seats, National won 42 and Labour 36; with the Greens on 16, ACT 13, NZ First 12 and Te Pāti Māori 5, Luxon's three-party bloc has 67 seats, one over the 66 needed. The new Opportunity party passed the 5% bar and wins 7 seats. About 400,000 special votes remain, and the official count ends November 27. Luxon said National is again the largest party but compromise will be needed; Hipkins said Labour is ready to govern if it gets the chance.
beats.means: The current government is most likely to stay, but its one-seat edge could vanish when special votes are counted, which in past elections have tended to favour the left. That leaves about three weeks of uncertainty over who governs.
beats.fx: Elections rarely move the New Zealand dollar much on their own. A likely return of the same government means little change in policy, but a slim, unsettled outcome is a small extra worry for a currency that was already the weakest of the majors on Friday.

impact.why: The same government looks likely to continue, but its one-seat majority hangs on special votes counted over the next three weeks.

items.watch: The official count on November 27: if special votes cost the right bloc a seat, coalition talks get harder and a change of government becomes possible.

items.headline: Trump says the US carried out new limited strikes on an Iranian air defense site on Friday, while talks continue
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: President Trump said US forces hit an Iranian air defense system on Friday, calling it a minor strike, and said Washington is still talking to Tehran. Iranian state media reported two blasts on Qeshm Island, near the Strait of Hormuz.

beats.was: The US and Israel have been at war with Iran since late February, and attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, have kept crude prices high. This week oil fell about 13% on hopes of a deal, and Iran is studying peace proposals carried by Qatar.
beats.happened: Speaking on Friday evening, Trump said the military had knocked out an Iranian anti-aircraft system in a short, limited strike, the first since Tuesday's US midterm elections. Iranian state media reported two explosions on Qeshm Island. Regional officials described a possible first step under the Qatari plan: the US would ease its blockade of Iranian ports and free some frozen funds, and Iran would let nuclear inspectors in and reopen Hormuz, though Washington has not agreed to the shipping terms.
beats.means: The US is pairing small military hits with diplomacy rather than choosing one, so the risk of a wider flare-up is back on the table even as the outline of a deal takes shape.
beats.fx: Markets are shut for the weekend. When trading resumes Sunday evening, the strike could add back some of the risk premium oil lost this week and draw some money to havens like the franc and gold, unless talks show clear progress first.

impact.why: A fresh US strike after a week of deal hopes puts supply risk back into crude prices.
More fighting tends to draw safe-haven money to the franc; Trump called the strike minor.
Gold usually gains when war risk rises, though the strike was small.
Dearer oil lifts Canada's export earnings.

items.watch: Whether Iran answers the strike, and whether the Qatari first-step plan is confirmed by Washington or Tehran before markets reopen Sunday evening.

items.headline: US-Iran talks show some progress, but Trump is also reported to be weighing fresh strikes as soon as Monday night
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Iran is reviewing Qatari proposals to limit its nuclear program in return for sanctions relief, but Fox News reported that President Trump discussed renewed strikes on Thursday, with the military said to favour November 9. Another tanker blast near the Strait of Hormuz was reported, with its crew safe.

beats.was: The US and Israel have been at war with Iran since late February, and attacks on shipping around the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, have kept crude prices high. Qatar is carrying messages between the two sides.
beats.happened: A US official and a diplomat said Iran's negotiators are studying Qatari proposals that would curb its nuclear work in exchange for easing sanctions. Ali Bagheri, a senior Iranian negotiator, said Tehran wants concrete US steps rather than promises on paper. Separately, Fox News reported Trump talked through new strikes on Thursday, and that military planners prefer the night of November 9. The UK's maritime security agency reported an explosion on a tanker near Hormuz.
beats.means: Talks and threats are running side by side, so the weekend could swing either way: a framework would point to more Gulf oil reaching the market, while new strikes would put the supply risk back in prices.
beats.fx: Oil ended the week near $98 a barrel for Brent, about 13% lower, largely on hopes of a deal. A strike would hit that hope and could lift crude and safe havens like the franc and gold when markets reopen Sunday evening.

impact.why: Signs of progress pull one way, a reported strike date the other; neither is confirmed.
New strikes would draw safe-haven money to the franc; a deal would ease that need.
Canada's oil earnings rise or fall with whichever way the Iran news breaks.

items.watch: Any US strikes on or around November 9, or a confirmed framework from Washington, Tehran or Qatar before markets reopen.

items.headline: New Zealand votes on Saturday, with most of the preliminary count due within hours of polls closing
items.story_title: New Zealand's 2026 general election
items.summary: New Zealanders elect a new parliament on Saturday November 7. Polls close at 7pm local time and most preliminary results should be in by late evening, though about a fifth of votes may be counted later.

beats.was: New Zealand holds a general election every three years. Over 1.5 million people voted early this time, and their ballots are counted first.
beats.happened: The Electoral Commission aims to report half of polling places by 10pm and 95% of the preliminary count by 11:30pm Saturday, New Zealand time (early Saturday morning US Central time). Special votes, just over 20% of the total in 2020, are counted later; the official result is due Friday November 27.
beats.means: A clear winner on the night would settle the question of who sets taxes and spending for the next three years. A close result could mean days or weeks of coalition talks, especially if special votes shift seats.
beats.fx: The New Zealand dollar was the weakest major currency on Friday, down about 1.2% against the US dollar. A drawn-out or uncertain result could add pressure when trading resumes Monday morning in Wellington.

impact.why: A preview: the direction depends on how clear the result is and what the winners plan for spending.

items.watch: Saturday night's preliminary count, and whether any party can form a government without long coalition talks.

items.headline: Euro-area shop sales fall 0.7% in September, far worse than expected, as the ECB's Lane urges caution
items.story_title: Will the ECB raise rates in December?
items.summary: Shoppers across the euro area spent 0.7% less in September than in August, a much bigger drop than forecast, after an even sharper fall in August. The European Central Bank's chief economist Philip Lane said rising energy costs must not spread into wages, but sounded cautious ahead of December.

beats.was: Inflation in the euro area is running at about 4% because of dearer energy from the Iran war, and the European Central Bank is weighing a rate rise in December. Higher prices have been squeezing household budgets.
beats.happened: Eurostat said retail sales fell 0.7% in September, against a forecast drop of 0.1%, and August was revised to a 2% fall. Compared with a year earlier, sales grew just 0.4%. ECB chief economist Philip Lane said policy must stop energy costs feeding into wages, but noted that borrowing conditions have already tightened and governments will likely spend less next year.
beats.means: Households are cutting back, which weakens the case for a December ECB rate rise. Lane's comments keep a rise possible but suggest the bank is in no hurry.
beats.fx: Weak spending and a cautious ECB weigh on the euro, which slipped against the yen on Friday.

impact.why: A much bigger drop in shop sales than expected, plus a cautious ECB chief economist, lowers the odds of a December rate rise.
The euro fell against the yen as Bank of Japan minutes kept a December rate rise in view.

items.watch: Euro-area inflation and wage figures before the ECB's December meeting, and whether other ECB officials echo Lane's caution.

items.headline: Markets now see about a 78% chance the Fed raises rates in December after the strong jobs report
items.story_title: Fed: the case for a December rate rise
items.summary: After Friday's jobs surprise, investors now put the odds of a Federal Reserve rate rise at its December 8–9 meeting near 78%, up from about 67% on Thursday. Several Fed officials said this week that inflation is still too high.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve held its rate at 3.75%–4% last week after raising it in September, and Chair Kevin Warsh said the next step would depend on how the data add up.
beats.happened: The US added 165,000 jobs in October, more than twice what was expected, and unemployment fell to 4.1%. Bets on a December rise jumped to about 85% right after the release before settling near 78%, and investors now expect the last rise of this cycle in April rather than June. St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem called inflation a tax that hits poorer households hardest.
beats.means: A December rise is now the market's main expectation, and the path of US rates looks a little higher and sooner than it did a day ago.
beats.fx: Higher expected US rates support the dollar and weigh on gold, which pays no interest.

impact.why: Firmer bets on a December Fed rise add support, though most of the move came with the jobs data itself.
Higher expected US rates raise the cost of holding gold.

items.watch: US inflation figures next week; a soft reading would pull December bets back down.

items.headline: Canadian business activity grew at a steady pace in October and hiring picked up, a survey shows
items.story_title: Bank of Canada: a rate rise to fight energy-driven inflation
items.summary: The Ivey survey of Canadian purchasing managers edged up to 58.3 in October, a solid pace of growth. Its hiring gauge rose and its prices gauge eased.

beats.was: Earlier on Friday Canada reported a second straight month of job losses, with unemployment up to 6.7%, which raised doubts about another Bank of Canada rate rise in December.
beats.happened: The Ivey purchasing managers index, which tracks business activity (above 50 means growth), rose to 58.3 in October from 58.2. Its employment measure climbed to 58.3 from 56.5, while its prices measure fell to 81.7 from 82.8.
beats.means: Businesses report steady growth and more hiring, a softer picture than the official jobs data but not enough to offset it. Slightly cooler price pressure fits a more cautious Bank of Canada.
beats.fx: A small offset to the weak jobs report for the Canadian dollar, which is mostly being driven by the stronger US dollar and oil prices today.

impact.why: Steady business growth and more hiring soften the blow from the weak jobs report.

items.watch: Canada's October inflation figures and whether the Bank of Canada signals a pause in December.

items.headline: German industrial output rises 0.7% in September, beating forecasts of no change
items.story_title: Germany's factory orders swing back
items.summary: Germany's factories produced 0.7% more in September than in August, when economists expected no change. The euro barely moved against the pound.

beats.was: German industry, the core of Europe's biggest economy, has been struggling with high energy costs. On Thursday, figures showed factory orders bounced 4.4% in September after a big drop in August.
beats.happened: Germany's statistics office said on Friday that industrial output rose 0.7% in September, led by cars and medicines, while construction and machinery fell. Compared with a year earlier, output was up just 0.4%.
beats.means: A better month for German factories, but the yearly gain is small and the stock-market sell-off is drowning out good news from Europe.
beats.fx: A mild plus for the euro that markets largely ignored, with the euro steady near 0.834 pounds.

impact.why: Output beat forecasts, though the yearly pace stays weak and traders paid it little attention.

items.watch: Euro-zone retail sales for September, and whether German orders and output keep rising in October.

items.headline: The dollar heads for its best day since June after strong US jobs data, and two Fed officials lean toward more rate rises
items.story_title: Fed: the case for a December rate rise
items.summary: The dollar index rose about 0.8% on Friday, its biggest one-day gain since mid-June, after a strong US jobs report. Two senior Federal Reserve officials said inflation is still too high, and markets now see about an 80% chance of a December rate rise.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve has been raising rates to fight inflation that dearer oil from the Iran war has pushed up. Earlier this week the dollar slipped after Democrats won control of Congress and a sell-off in AI stocks shook markets.
beats.happened: After the government reported 165,000 new jobs in October, far above the roughly 65,000 expected, the dollar index climbed to about 102.3. New York Fed president John Williams said inflation is too high, and San Francisco Fed president Mary Daly said more rate rises will likely be needed. The 2-year US Treasury yield rose to about 4.52%.
beats.means: Strong hiring plus officials openly talking about further rises make a December Fed rate rise the market's main expectation again, after doubts on Thursday.
beats.fx: Higher expected US rates lifted the dollar across the board: the euro fell to about $1.114, the pound to about $1.336 a day after the Bank of England's rate rise, and the yen weakened to about 158.4 per dollar.

impact.why: A jobs beat and Fed officials calling for more rises put a December hike back near 80% odds.
The euro gave back its gains for the week as US rates rose.
The pound slipped despite Thursday's Bank of England rise, as the dollar's pull was stronger.
A wider gap between US and Japanese rates weighs on the yen.

items.watch: US October inflation figures, out Tuesday November 10: a soft reading would cool talk of a December Fed rise.

items.headline: US chip stocks bounce about 4% after their worst day in over a year, while the 10-year US yield edges up to 4.86%
items.story_title: The AI-stock sell-off
items.summary: US stocks partly recovered on Friday after Thursday's steep fall in technology shares, led by a 4% bounce in chipmakers. Markets in Europe and Asia still ended lower, and money kept flowing into the dollar, yen and Swiss franc as safe places to wait.

beats.was: On Thursday the Nasdaq, the US index heavy in technology firms, fell about 5.5%, its worst day since April 2025, on worries that the new Democratic Congress will tighten rules on artificial-intelligence companies. Tokyo and Seoul fell about 6% on Friday.
beats.happened: On Friday the S&P 500 rose about 0.6% and the Nasdaq about 1.1%, and a chip-stock index gained about 4%, with Nvidia up about 4%. All three main US indexes were still set for a losing week. The 10-year US Treasury yield rose to about 4.86% after a stronger-than-expected jobs report.
beats.means: The panic eased but did not reverse: the bounce came only in the US, and investors still kept money in safe currencies. Higher US yields after the jobs data add a second reason to hold dollars.
beats.fx: The dollar gains on both safety demand and higher yields; the yen and franc keep some support from caution, while riskier currencies such as the Australian dollar get only modest relief.

impact.why: Safe-haven demand and a higher 10-year yield after strong jobs data both favour the dollar.
Caution still draws money to the yen, but the US stock bounce and higher US yields pull the other way.
The franc kept drawing safe-haven money as Europe's stocks fell over 1%.
A US stock bounce offers some relief, but Asian markets still fell hard.

items.watch: Whether the chip-stock bounce holds into next week, or the sell-off returns to Asia on Monday.

items.headline: Gold falls about 1% to near $4,050 after strong US jobs figures
items.story_title: Gold after the US midterms
items.summary: Gold slipped about 1% on Friday to near $4,050 an ounce after the US reported far more jobs than expected. It recovered a little when a consumer survey showed easing inflation expectations.

beats.was: Gold rose early this week as the dollar and US interest rates fell after Democrats won the US Congress, reaching about $4,145 an ounce on Thursday.
beats.happened: The US added 165,000 jobs in October, well above forecasts, and pay rose faster. Gold fell to about $4,048, down nearly 1% on the day, and bounced off its lows after the University of Michigan survey showed households expect less inflation.
beats.means: Strong jobs make a December Federal Reserve rate rise more likely. Higher rates raise the cost of holding gold, which pays no interest.
beats.fx: Gold is under pressure from a firmer dollar and higher US yields; analysts point to $4,000 as the next big level below.

impact.why: A strong jobs report raised the odds of a December Fed rise, weighing on gold.
The same jobs data lifted the dollar and US yields.

items.watch: Whether gold holds above $4,000, and Tuesday's US inflation figures.

items.headline: US consumer mood improved more than expected in early November, and people expect a little less inflation
items.story_title: Fed: the case for a December rate rise
items.summary: The University of Michigan's early November survey of US consumers rose to 51.0, above the 48 expected. Households now expect prices to rise 4.3% over the next year, down from 4.7%.

beats.was: US consumers have been gloomy all year, mainly because high prices are eating into living standards, and the Federal Reserve is weighing a December rate rise to bring inflation of about 3.7% down.
beats.happened: The University of Michigan's preliminary reading of consumer sentiment for November came in at 51.0 against about 48 expected. Expected inflation for the year ahead fell to 4.3% from 4.7%, and for the next five years to 3.4% from 3.5%. The survey's director said mood is still about 10% lower than in February.
beats.means: Shoppers are a bit less glum, which helps the growth outlook. Easing price expectations take a little pressure off the Fed, coming just after a strong jobs report that pushed the other way.
beats.fx: A firmer consumer backs the dollar slightly, but lower inflation expectations slightly soften the case for a December rate rise, so the net push on the dollar and gold is small.

impact.why: Better consumer mood helps, but lower expected inflation eases the pressure for a Fed rate rise.
Gold came off its lows after the release as inflation expectations eased.

items.watch: The final November reading later this month, and whether next week's US inflation figures confirm that price pressure is cooling.

items.headline: The pound and euro fall about 0.7% against the dollar after the strong US jobs report
items.story_title: Fed: the case for a December rate rise
items.summary: The dollar rose across the board after the US jobs report beat forecasts. The pound fell to about $1.336 and the euro to about $1.115, each down roughly 0.7%.

beats.was: The dollar had dropped to a one-month low this week after Democrats won the US Congress, and the pound had been helped by the Bank of England's first rate rise since 2023 on Thursday.
beats.happened: After the US reported 165,000 new jobs in October against about 70,000 expected, with faster pay growth, the pound slid from about $1.339 to $1.336 and the euro to $1.115. Short-term US Treasury yields rose. CIBC and Pantheon economists said they still expect the Federal Reserve to raise rates in December.
beats.means: The jobs data undid part of the dollar's post-election weakness and put the December Fed decision back at the centre of currency markets.
beats.fx: Pressure points toward a stronger dollar against the pound and euro for now; Tuesday's US inflation report is the next big test for that move.

impact.why: The pound gave back about 0.7% as the dollar rose on the jobs report.
Strong hiring and pay revived bets on a December Fed rise.
The euro fell about 0.6% to near $1.115 on the same dollar move.

items.watch: US consumer price figures on Tuesday; a soft reading could take the shine off the dollar's rebound.

items.headline: US employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far more than expected, and unemployment fell to 4.1%
items.story_title: Fed: the case for a December rate rise
items.summary: The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October, almost three times what economists expected, and the jobless rate dipped to 4.1%. Earlier months were also revised up and pay rose 0.4% in the month.

beats.was: US hiring had slowed to a crawl this year, with September first reported at just 29,000 new jobs. The Federal Reserve raised rates in September to fight inflation near 3.7%, and markets were weighing another rise in December after Thursday's stock crash and the Democrats' win in Congress.
beats.happened: The government's monthly jobs report showed 165,000 new jobs in October against about 60,000 expected, led by business services and health care. August and September were revised up by a combined 84,000, unemployment fell to 4.1% from 4.2%, and average hourly pay rose 0.4% on the month and 3.1% on the year.
beats.means: The US job market is much firmer than it looked, and faster pay growth adds to inflation worries. That makes it harder for the Fed to skip a December rate rise.
beats.fx: Strong jobs and firmer pay point to higher US rates for longer, which supports the dollar against the euro, yen and franc and tends to weigh on gold, which pays no interest.

impact.why: Jobs came in near three times the forecast, with upward revisions and faster pay, backing a December Fed rise.
Higher expected US rates make gold, which pays no interest, less attractive.
A wider gap between US and Japanese rates tends to pull the yen lower.

items.watch: How far markets raise the odds of a December Fed rate rise, and whether Fed officials point to this report in coming speeches.

items.headline: Canada lost 4,700 jobs in October and unemployment rose to 6.7%, a six-month high
items.story_title: Bank of Canada: a rate rise to fight energy-driven inflation
items.summary: Canada shed 4,700 jobs in October when economists expected a gain of about 13,600, and the jobless rate rose to 6.7% from 6.5%. Private employers cut about 52,500 jobs and wage growth slowed.

beats.was: Canada lost about 68,000 jobs in September. The Bank of Canada raised its rate to 2.50% in October, and Governor Tiff Macklem said this week more rises may be needed because dearer energy from the Iran war is lifting inflation.
beats.happened: Statistics Canada's monthly Labour Force Survey showed a second straight drop in jobs, with full-time work down about 18,000 and private-sector jobs falling for the first time since February. Unemployment reached 6.7%, the highest since April, and hourly pay for permanent staff grew 2.0% on the year, down from 2.3%.
beats.means: Hiring in Canada keeps weakening while pay growth cools, which gives the Bank of Canada a reason to go slower on further rate rises.
beats.fx: A weaker job market lowers the odds of more Canadian rate rises, which weighs on the Canadian dollar, especially next to a much stronger US jobs report released at the same moment.

impact.why: A surprise job loss and a jump in unemployment weaken the case for another Bank of Canada rise.

items.watch: Whether Bank of Canada officials soften their talk of more rate rises after a second weak jobs month.

items.headline: Oil swings near $100 as Iran says it could reopen Hormuz within two days if the US lifts sanctions
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Brent crude moved back toward $100 a barrel on Friday after reports of new tanker attacks near the Strait of Hormuz. A senior Iranian official said the strait could reopen within two days if Washington lifts oil sanctions and frees Iranian assets.

beats.was: The US-Iran war has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil. Brent fell from about $104 to near $94 this week on hopes the new Democratic Congress pushes for peace, and Qatar is mediating between the two sides.
beats.happened: Brent rose to near $99.90 early Friday as Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed mines destroyed four tankers south of Hormuz, a claim not confirmed by others. Iran is studying nuclear proposals passed on by Qatar, and an Iranian official said Hormuz could reopen in two days if the US meets its demands. President Trump said there were no immediate plans to strike Iran but did not rule it out.
beats.means: Oil is pulled two ways: a possible deal that would free up supply, and ongoing attacks that keep it scarce. JPMorgan estimates the world was already oversupplied by 1.4 million barrels a day in October.
beats.fx: Big swings in oil feed through to oil-linked currencies like the Canadian dollar, and to importers like the yen, which suffer when crude is dear.

impact.why: New tanker attacks lift prices while a conditional offer to reopen Hormuz points to more supply later.
Canada's biggest export swings with each headline from the Gulf.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so dearer crude weighs on the yen and cheaper crude helps.

items.watch: Any US reply to Iran's sanctions demand, and independent confirmation of the tanker attacks.

items.headline: Brent slips back to about $97.50 after briefly topping $100, on track for its worst week since early 2020
items.story_title: Oil and the Iran war after the US midterms
items.summary: Brent crude fell about 0.8% to near $97.55 a barrel on Friday morning in Europe, giving up an early climb above $100. It is heading for a fall of about 16% this week.

beats.was: Oil prices had jumped this year because the Iran war choked shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil. After Democrats won both houses of the US Congress on Tuesday, Brent fell 8% on Wednesday on hopes Washington pushes to end the war.
beats.happened: Brent briefly rose above $100 early on Friday as more tankers were attacked near Hormuz, then slipped back to about $97.55; US crude was near $89.80. A 16% weekly drop would be Brent's steepest since the start of the Covid pandemic and its biggest in dollar terms in records back to 1988.
beats.means: Ship attacks still put a floor under prices, but the bigger force this week is the bet that more Middle East oil will reach the market and that supply may soon outrun demand.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil eases pressure on big importers like Japan and the euro area and weighs on the Canadian dollar, which leans on oil exports.

impact.why: On track for its steepest weekly fall since early 2020 on hopes of more Middle East supply.
Oil is Canada's main export, so a lower price takes away some support.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so cheaper crude eases a drag on the yen.

items.watch: Any US answer to Iran's proposal sent through Qatar, and whether tanker attacks near Hormuz keep rising.

items.headline: US and Iran move closer to a possible breakthrough in talks to end the war, Bloomberg reports
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Iran is studying nuclear proposals passed on by Qatar and is willing to discuss issues it had refused before, a diplomat told Bloomberg. Neither government has confirmed a deal, and Iran still sets steep conditions.

beats.was: The US and Israel have been at war with Iran since late February, disrupting oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Peace talks, mediated by Qatar, have stalled since an earlier ceasefire framework collapsed, and the White House has warned President Trump is weighing new strikes.
beats.happened: A diplomat familiar with the talks said Iran is reviewing Qatari proposals on its nuclear program and is open to topics it had ruled out. An Iranian official said real talks start only after the US meets seven demands, including lifting sanctions, releasing frozen assets and paying war damages. Trump spoke with Qatar's ruler, Emir Sheikh Tamim, and said things were going very well with Iran.
beats.means: This is the clearest sign yet that both sides might find a path to end the war, but it rests on one unnamed source and Iran's conditions remain far apart from Washington's.
beats.fx: Hopes of a deal pulled Brent crude back below $100 on Friday, leaving it about 13% lower for the week. Cheaper oil helps importers like the yen and weighs on the Canadian dollar, Canada's biggest export being crude.

impact.why: A deal would free up Gulf supply, but the report is unconfirmed.
Lower oil prices cut into Canada's main export earnings.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so cheaper crude eases pressure on the yen.

items.watch: Any confirmation from Washington or Tehran that formal talks have restarted, or a US move on sanctions; new strikes or tanker attacks would undo it.

items.headline: Stock sell-off spreads to Europe after the worst US chip-stock drop since 2020
items.story_title: AI stocks sell off after the US midterms
items.summary: European stocks opened lower on Friday, joining Asia in a sell-off that began when US chip shares had their worst day since 2020. Seoul's Kospi fell almost 9% at one point and trading there was briefly halted.

beats.was: After Democrats won the US Congress on Tuesday, investors began to fear tougher rules on the huge data centres that power artificial intelligence, including a proposal from Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to pause new ones.
beats.happened: On Thursday a US index of chip companies fell about 12%, its biggest one-day drop since 2020, and the S&P 500 lost about $2.9 trillion in value. On Friday Tokyo's Nikkei fell as much as 7%, Seoul's Kospi dropped almost 9% with a 20-minute trading halt, and European markets opened lower.
beats.means: The sell-off is now global, so worries about AI spending are feeding a wider pullback from risk rather than staying a US tech story.
beats.fx: A broad flight from stocks tends to help the Swiss franc and yen as safe places to park money and to hurt currencies tied to global growth, such as the Australian and New Zealand dollars.

impact.why: Investors leaving stocks often move money into the franc.
The Australian dollar tends to fall when global stocks slide.
A global sell-off draws some safety buying into the yen.

items.watch: Whether US stocks steady on Friday after Thursday's crash, or the sell-off deepens into a second day.

items.headline: Gold falls about 1% to near $4,044 as oil's rebound revives inflation worries; Goldman lowers its forecast
items.story_title: Gold after the US midterms
items.summary: Gold dropped about 1.1% to near $4,044 an ounce in Asian trading on Friday, though it is still heading for its best week since late August. Goldman Sachs cut its end-2026 forecast to $4,150 from $4,650.

beats.was: Gold jumped about 3.5% on Wednesday after Democrats won the US Congress and the dollar and US yields fell, and reached about $4,145 on Thursday. Gold tends to struggle when interest rates are expected to stay high, because it pays no interest.
beats.happened: Spot gold fell 1.1% on Friday as oil climbed back toward $100, reviving fears that inflation keeps US rates high for longer. Some investors also sold gold to cover losses in the stock sell-off. Futures give about a 68% chance the Federal Reserve raises rates in December.
beats.means: The midterm bounce in gold is being tested: dearer oil and the risk of a December Fed rise pull against it, and a big bank has turned less upbeat on where the price ends the year.
beats.fx: Gold faces downward pressure for now; Friday's US jobs report will shape the Fed outlook that is driving it.

impact.why: Fell about 1% on renewed inflation and rate worries, and Goldman cut its year-end forecast.
Higher-for-longer rate talk helps it, while the stock rout keeps December Fed bets below where they were.

items.watch: The US jobs report for October, due Friday at 7:30 AM CT, and how it moves the odds of a December Fed rise.

items.headline: Yen touches a one-week high near 157.4 per dollar as the stock rout spreads; markets trim bets on a December Fed rate rise
items.story_title: AI stocks sell off after the US midterms
items.summary: The yen and Swiss franc each rose about 0.2% against the dollar in Asian trading on Friday as stocks slid. Futures now give about a 70% chance the Federal Reserve raises rates in December, down from over 80% on Wednesday.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve has been raising US interest rates to fight inflation pushed up by dearer oil from the Iran war, and markets expected another rise in December. Democrats won both houses of Congress on Tuesday, and on Thursday the Nasdaq had its worst day since April 2025.
beats.happened: In Asia on Friday the yen briefly reached 157.40 per dollar, its strongest in a week, before giving some back. The two-year US Treasury yield fell about 0.1 point to 4.47%, and the dollar index held flat near 101.55.
beats.means: Investors now see a smaller chance of a December Fed rise, which takes some support away from the dollar. At the same time, fear in stock markets brings in money looking for safety, so the two forces roughly cancel out.
beats.fx: Lower US yields and safety buying help the yen and franc; the dollar is steady, not falling, and Friday's October jobs report will decide which force wins.

impact.why: Safety buying and lower US yields lifted it to a one-week high, though the gain partly faded.
Fewer bets on a December Fed rise weigh on it, while safety demand holds it up.
Rose about 0.2% as investors looked for a safe place for money.

items.watch: The US jobs report for October, due Friday at 7:30 AM CT.

items.headline: Brent rises toward $100 for a second day, but is still set for a 12% weekly fall
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Brent crude rose about 1.6% to near $99.90 a barrel early on Friday, its second daily gain, as tanker attacks near Hormuz continue. It is still on track to end the week about 12% lower.

beats.was: The US and Israel have been at war with Iran for about nine months, and Iran controls shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for Gulf oil. Oil fell 8% on Wednesday to a two-month low on bets that the new Democratic Congress pushes Washington to end the war.
beats.happened: By early Friday Brent was up $1.57 at about $99.86 and US crude up about 1.2% at $91.62. Iran said three more tankers were attacked near Hormuz on Thursday, and attacks are running near a record pace.
beats.means: Wednesday's plunge looks like it went too far for some buyers, since actual supply through Hormuz has not improved. Hopes for peace pull prices down, while each new attack pushes them back up.
beats.fx: Dearer oil helps the Canadian dollar and Norway's crown and weighs on big importers such as Japan; the weekly fall still leaves oil well below last week's levels.

impact.why: A second day of gains on tanker attacks, after a steep weekly fall.
Oil is Canada's biggest export, so higher prices help the currency.
Japan buys almost all its oil abroad, so dearer crude weighs on the yen.

items.watch: Whether more tankers are hit near Hormuz, and any US response to Iran's nuclear proposal sent through Qatar.

items.headline: Japan's Nikkei falls more than 6% and South Korea's Kospi about 7% as the AI-stock sell-off spreads to Asia
items.story_title: AI stocks sell off after the US midterms
items.summary: Tokyo's Nikkei 225 fell more than 6% and Seoul's Kospi about 7% early on Friday, following Wall Street's worst day in over a year. The yen barely moved, near 157.8 per dollar.

beats.was: Democrats won both houses of the US Congress on Tuesday, raising worries about tighter rules on artificial intelligence and slower building of data centres. On Thursday the Nasdaq fell 5.5% and the S&P 500 4.4% as chip shares crashed.
beats.happened: In Friday morning trading the Nikkei dropped about 6.2% and the Kospi about 7.1%, both heavy in chip and tech makers. Australia's ASX 200 fell a milder 0.7%. US 10-year yields eased to about 4.84%.
beats.means: The sell-off has moved from New York to Asia's tech-heavy markets, so worry about global growth is spreading. Falls this big usually pull money toward safer assets and away from growth-linked currencies.
beats.fx: The yen held near 157.8 per dollar rather than jumping, as dearer oil still weighs on Japan; the Korean won and the Australian dollar are the most exposed.

impact.why: Safe-haven pull and lower US yields help, but the yen hardly moved as Tokyo stocks sank.
Asia's stock slump adds to Thursday's hit to the most growth-linked major currency.
Tends to fall with the Australian dollar when risk appetite drops.
Investors tend to park money in the franc during steep stock sell-offs.

items.watch: Whether European and US stocks steady on Friday, and the US jobs report for October at 7:30 AM CT.
